data.name: Generalise Pythagoras
data.narration: For every right angled triangle, the squares on the two shorter sides have the same total area as the square on the longest side. That is Pythagoras theorem.
data.prompt: Would this area relationship hold for a triangle with no right angle?

steps.name: Start with the right angle
steps.narration: This triangle has one right angle. The two sides meeting there are the shorter legs. The longest side lies opposite that angle.
steps.prompt: Where is the right angle? Which side is opposite it?

steps.name: Square on the first leg
steps.narration: Construct a square on side a. Every edge of this square has length a. Its area is a squared.
steps.prompt: Why is the square area a multiplied by a?

steps.name: Square on the second leg
steps.narration: Build another square on side b. Its area is b squared. The two smaller squares have different areas.
steps.prompt: Which square has the greater area? Why?

steps.name: Square on the hypotenuse
steps.narration: The longest side is c, opposite the right angle. A square with side c has an area of c squared.
steps.prompt: Why is the green square tilted? Does tilting change its area?

steps.name: Count the small squares
steps.narration: Count the unit squares on both shorter sides. A side of length a makes a times a square units; the other gives b times b.
steps.prompt: How many unit squares cover each smaller square?

steps.name: Compare the total area
steps.narration: Add the two shorter side square areas. You will get precisely the same area as the tilted square on the hypotenuse.
steps.prompt: What area is covered by both smaller squares together?

steps.name: One enclosing square
steps.narration: Here is a bigger square of side a plus b. Four identical right triangles leave a central square whose area is c squared.
steps.prompt: What is the side length of the middle tilted square?

steps.name: Rearrange the same pieces
steps.narration: Move the same four triangles to new positions inside an equally sized square. The uncovered spaces are now an a squared square and a b squared square.
steps.prompt: Has the total area of the outer square changed?

steps.name: The remaining areas must match
steps.narration: Both large squares have the same area, and the four triangles in each have the same total area. So what remains must match: a squared plus b squared equals c squared.
steps.prompt: Why are we allowed to compare the uncovered areas?

data.narration: Name the hypotenuse, square the known lengths, add or subtract the areas, then square root. That method works for many right triangle problems.

steps.name: Locate the right angle
steps.narration: Start with the marked right angle. This rule only applies to right angled triangles.
steps.prompt: Where do the two shorter sides meet?

steps.name: Identify the hypotenuse
steps.narration: The hypotenuse always sits opposite the right angle. It is the longest side, even if the triangle is tilted.
steps.prompt: Which labelled side faces the right angle?

steps.name: Read the known lengths
steps.narration: Mark the sides that are given. Keep the missing side as a question mark rather than guessing it.
steps.prompt: Are we finding the longest side or one of the two shorter sides?

steps.name: Build square areas
steps.narration: Square a length to find the area of the square built on that side. We work with areas before lengths.
steps.prompt: Which square areas can you calculate from the given lengths?

steps.name: Choose addition or subtraction
steps.narration: If the longest side is missing, add the two smaller square areas. If a shorter side is missing, subtract its partner square area from the largest area.
steps.prompt: Which calculation makes the missing square area?

steps.name: Square the known values
steps.narration: Multiply each known side length by itself. Do not add plain side lengths together.
steps.prompt: Which numbers are square areas and which are lengths?

steps.name: Calculate the missing area
steps.narration: Apply the area equation to calculate the missing square area. This is not yet the side length.
steps.prompt: What operation gives the missing square area?

steps.name: Isolate the missing square
steps.narration: Put the unknown squared on its own. Check that the area is positive and smaller than the largest square area when finding a shorter side.
steps.prompt: What does the squared symbol tell us about this value?

steps.name: Take the positive square root
steps.narration: A side length is the positive square root of its square area. Always give a length, not an area.
steps.prompt: Why do we take a positive square root?

steps.name: Check the full relationship
steps.narration: Check the answer by squaring all three side lengths. The two smaller areas must add to the largest.
steps.prompt: Does the answer satisfy the original theorem?

steps.name: Apply to a real situation
steps.narration: The same right triangle might be a ladder, a ramp, or a diagonal across a space. Identify the right angle first.
steps.prompt: Where are the perpendicular sides in the real scene?

steps.name: Find the square corner
steps.narration: Trigonometric ratios start with a right angled triangle. Locate the marked square corner first.
steps.prompt: Where are the perpendicular sides?

steps.name: Choose a reference angle
steps.narration: The orange angle is our reference angle theta. The side names depend on this chosen angle.
steps.prompt: Which acute angle are we using?

steps.name: Meet the hypotenuse
steps.narration: The hypotenuse is the longest side opposite the right angle. It never changes its role.
steps.prompt: Which side runs across the square corner?

steps.name: Name the opposite side
steps.narration: The opposite side sits across from the orange angle. It never touches that angle.
steps.prompt: Which side does not touch the orange angle?

steps.name: Name the adjacent side
steps.narration: The adjacent side touches the orange angle, but it is not the hypotenuse.
steps.prompt: Which shorter side forms the orange angle?

steps.name: Build the sine ratio
steps.narration: Sine of theta is opposite divided by hypotenuse. The length numbers form a ratio, not an addition.
steps.prompt: Which length belongs on top of the sine fraction?

steps.name: Build the cosine ratio
steps.narration: Cosine of theta is adjacent divided by hypotenuse. The hypotenuse stays on the bottom.
steps.prompt: What changes from sine to cosine?

steps.name: Build the tangent ratio
steps.narration: Tangent of theta is opposite divided by adjacent. The hypotenuse is not used here.
steps.prompt: Why is the hypotenuse absent from tangent?

steps.name: Compare similar triangles
steps.narration: Doubling every side changes the lengths, but not the angle or its ratios. The divisions give the same result.
steps.prompt: Why do similar right triangles keep identical trig ratios?

steps.name: Use a ratio to find a side
steps.narration: Choose the ratio containing your known side and unknown side. Rearrange the equation before calculating.
steps.prompt: Do you need to multiply or divide to isolate the missing side?

steps.name: Check using side and angle
steps.narration: Check that sine and cosine lie between zero and one for acute angles, and the hypotenuse remains longest.
steps.prompt: Is the result sensible for this triangle?

steps.name: The right-angle landmark
steps.narration: Pythagoras and trigonometry start with a right angled triangle. The little square marks the fixed ninety degree corner.
steps.prompt: Find the square corner before doing any ratio.

steps.name: Choose our angle
steps.narration: Theta is the orange angle between the blue base and green hypotenuse. Changing theta will change the triangle.
steps.prompt: Which corner is theta?

steps.name: Adjacent touches theta
steps.narration: The adjacent side is the shorter blue side next to theta. The hypotenuse also touches theta, but it is a separate role.
steps.prompt: Which shorter side touches theta?

steps.name: Opposite faces theta
steps.narration: The purple opposite side lies across from theta. It does not touch the orange angle.
steps.prompt: Which side faces the chosen angle?

steps.name: Hypotenuse never changes role
steps.narration: The long green side faces the right angle. We will keep its length fixed while we change theta.
steps.prompt: How can both shorter sides change while the longest stays fixed?

steps.name: Sweep the acute angle
steps.narration: As the angle grows, the triangle gets taller and less wide. The fixed green hypotenuse anchors the sweep.
steps.prompt: Which leg gets longer when theta increases?

steps.name: Sine comes from opposite
steps.narration: Sine theta equals opposite divided by hypotenuse. With a fixed hypotenuse, sine increases as theta grows.
steps.prompt: What happens to sine when opposite becomes longer?

steps.name: Cosine comes from adjacent
steps.narration: Cosine theta equals adjacent divided by hypotenuse. With a fixed hypotenuse, cosine decreases as theta grows.
steps.prompt: What happens to cosine as the base shrinks?

steps.name: Tangent compares two legs
steps.narration: Tangent theta equals opposite divided by adjacent. As one grows and the other shrinks, tangent rises rapidly.
steps.prompt: Why does tangent change faster at larger angles?

steps.name: Read the ratio table
steps.narration: Each row is one angle. Read its sine, cosine and tangent in the same row. All the values come from actual triangle ratios.
steps.prompt: Which table column gets smaller as the angle increases?

steps.name: Spot the pattern
steps.narration: Sine rises and cosine falls as the acute angle increases. At forty five degrees they are equal.
steps.prompt: What makes sine and cosine equal at forty five degrees?

steps.name: Scale does not change ratios
steps.narration: If every side becomes twice as long, the angle and all three side ratios stay exactly the same.
steps.prompt: Why does doubling both numbers in a fraction keep the ratio?

steps.name: Reverse the ratio
steps.narration: Inverse sine, inverse cosine and inverse tangent find the angle from a known ratio. First choose the correct pair of sides.
steps.prompt: If opposite and hypotenuse are known, which inverse ratio finds theta?

steps.name: Check and transfer
steps.narration: Work in degrees, match the sides to theta, divide in the right order, then use the inverse function to recover the angle.
steps.prompt: Does your angle agree with how tall or wide the triangle looks?

data.say: Try moving the point. Before looking at the values, predict the signs from the quadrant.

steps.name: A circle of radius one
steps.say: This is a circle centred at the origin. Every point on the circumference is exactly one unit from the centre.

steps.name: Angles start on positive x
steps.say: Zero degrees starts on the positive horizontal axis. We measure positive angles anticlockwise.

steps.name: Turn through thirty degrees
steps.say: Rotate the radius anticlockwise by thirty degrees. Its length stays exactly one.

steps.name: Drop the vertical projection
steps.say: Drop a perpendicular from the point to the horizontal axis. The foot completes a right angled triangle.

steps.name: Horizontal coordinate is cosine
steps.say: Cosine is the signed horizontal coordinate. In quadrant one it is positive.

steps.name: Vertical coordinate is sine
steps.say: Sine is the signed vertical coordinate. Here it is also positive.

steps.name: Read the ordered pair
steps.say: The point has coordinates cosine theta, then sine theta. Horizontal comes first, vertical second.

steps.name: Pythagoras still holds
steps.say: The legs form a right triangle with hypotenuse one. Cosine squared plus sine squared equals one.

steps.name: Ninety-degree landmark
steps.say: At ninety degrees cosine is zero and sine is one. The point sits at the very top.

steps.name: Quadrant two: negative x
steps.say: Beyond ninety degrees the horizontal coordinate turns negative while the vertical coordinate stays positive.

steps.name: One hundred eighty degrees
steps.say: At one hundred eighty degrees, the point is negative one, zero.

steps.name: Quadrant three: both negative
steps.say: In quadrant three both coordinates are negative. Cosine and sine keep their signed meanings.

steps.name: Two hundred seventy degrees
steps.say: At two hundred seventy degrees cosine is zero and sine is negative one.

steps.name: Quadrant four: positive x

data.name: Choose the appropriate triangle

steps.name: A three-dimensional journey
steps.say: A cuboid has length, width and height. The longest route inside joins opposite corners.

steps.name: Measure three perpendicular edges
steps.say: Length, width and height are perpendicular dimensions. Start with the flat base.

steps.name: Find the rectangle on the floor
steps.say: The floor is a rectangle with its length and width at right angles.

steps.name: Draw its base diagonal
steps.say: Join two opposite floor corners. This is the hypotenuse of our first right triangle.

steps.name: Square the floor lengths
steps.say: Square the length and the width. Their sum is the square of the base diagonal.

steps.name: Take the first square root
steps.say: Square root the area sum to reveal the exact base diagonal.

steps.name: Rise vertically from the far corner
steps.say: The height is perpendicular to the entire floor, including its diagonal.

steps.name: See a second right triangle
steps.say: The base diagonal and vertical height make the shorter sides of a second right triangle.

steps.name: Join the opposite cuboid corners
steps.say: Now draw the space diagonal, the straight line through the box.

steps.name: Pythagoras for the space diagonal
steps.say: The space diagonal squared is the base diagonal squared plus the height squared.

steps.name: Combine both triangles
steps.say: Substitute the floor calculation and obtain length squared plus width squared plus height squared.

steps.name: Find the space distance
steps.say: Square root the three squared edges. Keep precision until the final calculation.

steps.name: Identify the elevation angle
steps.say: The angle of elevation is between the floor diagonal and the space diagonal.

steps.name: Opposite and adjacent
steps.say: Height is opposite the elevation angle, and the floor diagonal is adjacent.

steps.name: Build the tangent relationship
steps.say: Tangent of the elevation angle equals height divided by the floor diagonal.

steps.name: Invert tangent to find the angle
steps.say: Inverse tangent gives the angle, in degrees, from those two lengths.

steps.name: Rearrange to find a missing height
steps.say: If the space diagonal is given, subtract the floor diagonal squared and take a square root.

STEPS.name: Build from a square or equilateral triangle
STEPS.prompt: Look for the parent shape: square or equilateral triangle.

STEPS.name: Make the accurate diagonal or altitude
STEPS.prompt: Split the parent shape with a precisely placed line.

STEPS.name: Confirm the right angle
STEPS.prompt: Find the 90-degree angle made by the split.

STEPS.name: Compare side lengths
STEPS.prompt: Which sides are equal, and which side is longest?

STEPS.name: Derive the missing root
STEPS.prompt: Use Pythagoras to find the exact length containing a square root.

STEPS.name: Choose the reference angle
STEPS.prompt: 30°, 60°, or 45° — angle choice determines opposite and adjacent.

STEPS.name: Name opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse
STEPS.prompt: Opposite faces the chosen angle. Hypotenuse faces the right angle.

STEPS.name: Write sine as an exact fraction
STEPS.prompt: Opposite divided by hypotenuse. Keep the surd exact.

STEPS.name: Write cosine as an exact fraction
STEPS.prompt: Adjacent divided by hypotenuse. Do not swap side roles.

STEPS.name: Write tangent as an exact fraction
STEPS.prompt: Opposite divided by adjacent, with a rationalised form when appropriate.

STEPS.name: Compare and generalise
STEPS.prompt: Side ratios stay the same even if the triangle changes size.

sample.say: Our right triangle will come from an equilateral triangle, where each whole side has length two.
